10c3aaf71e.q: What is Tarleton's founding year and how has the company evolved through multiple generations?
10c3aaf71e.a: Tarleton was founded in 1946, right after World War II, when Dirk's grandfather and three other partners purchased an existing company that was essentially defunct. They bought the land and the name, and after some of the older partners retired, Dirk's grandfather bought them out. Dirk's father transitioned as the second generation, and now Dirk represents the third generation with a fourth generation—his daughter and nephew—already working at the company.
10c3aaf71e.e: Creating a Culture of Safety That Lasts

73bb293462.q: How has Tarleton's approach to safety evolved from physical safety to a broader safe and caring environment?
73bb293462.a: Tarleton's core values—safety, quality, integrity, and enthusiasm—were documented in the mid-1970s, and the company held its first safety banquet in 1964, before OSHA was even established. Initially, safety focused on physical hazards like falls and hard hats. However, in recent years, Tarleton morphed its safety core value into building a safe and caring environment to encompass mental safety, community relations, and work-life balance, reflecting broader organizational understanding of worker wellbeing.
73bb293462.e: Creating a Culture of Safety That Lasts

70e5ab042a.q: What role does team accountability play in Tarleton's safety culture according to AGC of America conferences?
70e5ab042a.a: According to sessions Dirk attended at the AGC of America national conference in mid-March, one of the strongest takeaways centered on team effort in safety. Dirk emphasizes that Tarleton's number-one tool in the tool belt is each other, and helping teams hold themselves and individuals accountable to one another goes a long way in building a strong safety culture. This approach addresses how office leadership can communicate safety hazards that resonate with front-line workers who face day-to-day exposures.
70e5ab042a.e: Creating a Culture of Safety That Lasts

05a4a74874.q: What is the ASSIST program and how does it address mental health in construction?
05a4a74874.a: Tarleton developed ASSIST in conjunction with Washington University, modifying a program originally developed in Australia called Mates. ASSIST trains multiple levels of communicators with skills to speak to someone going through a rough time, or to someone who knows someone struggling. This addresses the fact that construction is the number two industry for deaths by suicide and has significant drug addiction prevalence.
05a4a74874.e: Creating a Culture of Safety That Lasts

47b00ce6fb.q: What specific equipment improvements has Tarleton implemented to ensure safety for women workers?
47b00ce6fb.a: Tarleton obtained a grant to provide safety harnesses that properly fit women workers. The company has also adopted new-style hard hats with chin straps that hold the head better, and suppliers are now adapting equipment for different scenarios—reducing weight, adding sun protection, and accommodating flashlights and face shields—ensuring equipment fits all body types appropriately.
47b00ce6fb.e: Creating a Culture of Safety That Lasts

347776c545.q: How is artificial intelligence being used to identify safety trends and incident correlations in construction?
347776c545.a: Tarleton has started using AI tools to analyze trends in safety incidents more easily. The company examines correlations across incidents—for instance, analyzing ten incidents to identify salient facts and patterns. Dirk notes that it was previously difficult to draw trends because every incident is slightly different, but new AI tools are making it easier to spot meaningful connections and improve safety responses.
347776c545.e: Creating a Culture of Safety That Lasts

f2576e7535.q: What percentage of job-related construction accidents does OSHA attribute to language barriers?
f2576e7535.a: OSHA says 25 percent of job-related accidents are attributed to language barriers. However, Monique Lewis notes this number is likely underreported, as many incidents go unreported entirely when workers lack the language to report them or don't feel safe doing so.
f2576e7535.e: Language Truly is PPE: Language Risk Mitigation on the Jobsite

1fb38862e5.q: What percentage of Hispanic workers does Monique Lewis observe on construction job sites compared to official statistics?
1fb38862e5.a: Official numbers tell us 33 percent of construction workers are Hispanic, but Monique Lewis observes when passing work zones daily that she is seeing 50 to 60 percent Hispanic faces on construction sites, suggesting the actual demographic presence is significantly higher than reported statistics.
1fb38862e5.e: Language Truly is PPE: Language Risk Mitigation on the Jobsite

084c3b57c3.q: How long did it take a safety director to see measurable improvement after joining Monique Lewis's language training program?
084c3b57c3.a: A safety director who had worked with a Spanish-speaking crew for about six months was only in Monique Lewis's program for about seven weeks. During that time, he was able to recognize and address a situation where a Hispanic worker reported his harness had been damaged and he had needed one for months but lacked the English comfort level to report it.
084c3b57c3.e: Language Truly is PPE: Language Risk Mitigation on the Jobsite

f499ed86b3.q: What is Next2Native's mission regarding language in construction safety?
f499ed86b3.a: Next2Native's mission is to bring language to the same level of importance in the construction industry's mind as a hard hat. The company operates under the theme that language is PPE (personal protective equipment), and language truly is PPE because it protects workers just as much as physical equipment does.
f499ed86b3.e: Language Truly is PPE: Language Risk Mitigation on the Jobsite

e3686b3a8e.q: What bilingual communication gap exists in construction toolbox talks and OSHA training delivery?
e3686b3a8e.a: Many companies conduct toolbox talks and OSHA trainings entirely in English without bilingual instruction available. Monique Lewis describes a case where an OSHA instructor delivered fall protection training completely in English to a crew that included three Spanish-speaking Hispanic workers; all gave thumbs up at the end, but moments later one worker tied a rope around his waist and climbed to height—revealing he had not understood the training.
e3686b3a8e.e: Language Truly is PPE: Language Risk Mitigation on the Jobsite

1d6f3a345d.q: Why does using a bilingual foreman alone not fully solve language barriers on construction job sites?
1d6f3a345d.a: A bilingual foreman acting as the sole translator for 30 to 50 percent of a crew becomes overwhelmed, unable to perform their primary job duties, and their mental bandwidth is consumed by translating. Additionally, they become aware of private HR issues they should not know about, and if an injured non-English speaker needs medical care, the foreman leaves the crew without a liaison.
1d6f3a345d.e: Language Truly is PPE: Language Risk Mitigation on the Jobsite

efc2542b08.q: What is the gender pay gap in non-union construction compared to union scale positions?
efc2542b08.a: In the non-union sector, women earn approximately 84 cents on the dollar compared to men who get paid considerably more. In contrast, union positions operate on standardized scales: first-year apprentices earn about 60% to 65% of the journeyman scale, then progress year by year to the full journeyman rate. However, women in management roles like project managers, field engineers, and project superintendents still do not receive equal pay for the same work as their male counterparts, even in union environments.
efc2542b08.e: Restoring Respect & Rebuilding the Future of the Trades

47be2f419c.q: What are the entry-level wage expectations for apprentices in construction trades?
47be2f419c.a: A first-year apprentice in union trades typically earns 60% to 65% of the journeyman scale, which these days is a pretty good wage to earn per hour. Journeyman wages nowadays, factoring in a little overtime, can easily reach $80,000 to $100,000 a year, plus benefits including an annuity or 401k and sometimes a vacation fund.
47be2f419c.e: Restoring Respect & Rebuilding the Future of the Trades

1a6aa8a16b.q: Why do women perform better at welding jobs in the construction trades according to job site observations?
1a6aa8a16b.a: Women tend to be more meticulous and know how to slow down and do the job carefully, making them skilled welders. Even men on job sites acknowledge this, saying women are just better welders because they take their time, whereas men often want to get in there, get it done, and move on to the next one. This applies across harder trades like boilermakers, ironworkers, and pipe fitters.
1a6aa8a16b.e: Restoring Respect & Rebuilding the Future of the Trades

3b2a5313d6.q: What role did the removal of shop classes from high school curriculum play in the construction workforce pipeline?
3b2a5313d6.a: High schools used to offer metalworking, architectural drafting, shop class, woodworking, and automotive classes. Teachers could identify kids with real skills for mechanics or drafting. The removal of these classes has been devastating for youth because guidance counselors continue pushing college exclusively, even though college is not for everybody and the trades offer viable career paths.
3b2a5313d6.e: Restoring Respect & Rebuilding the Future of the Trades

5464aa5306.q: What strategies should construction company leaders use to recruit and retain women in the field?
5464aa5306.a: Construction company leaders should attend career fairs with booths and hands-on presentations showing what they do and what kind of people they look for. Smaller contractors doing well with retention should recruit kids on Saturdays to show them exactly what they do. Companies should also partner with programs like Habitat for Humanity to let families get hands-on experience. Executive presence at career days, showing kids real work environments safely, helps demystify construction and builds interest from a young age.
5464aa5306.e: Restoring Respect & Rebuilding the Future of the Trades

529c149c7d.q: How does the construction trade pathway provide economic security for single parent families compared to other careers?
529c149c7d.a: Single-parent women are highly encouraged to enter the trades because they will earn a living wage even as apprentices, and they receive insurance which makes a big difference in reducing financial burden. However, disparate equal opportunity persists when employers assume mothers will take days off if a child gets sick, creating workplace bias that is hard to overcome despite women having jobs too.
529c149c7d.e: Restoring Respect & Rebuilding the Future of the Trades
